Clark Kent: probably a kitbash with maybe a new face print Lois Lane: probably a kitbash Jimmy Olsen: definitely a kitbash, my only hope is they don’t give him the Professor Xavier head Supergirl: probably going to be the red skirt version, although I’d love to see the white shirt version or the blue skirt version just to give some variety from the last version Mr Terrific: Really hoping he has printed legs and I think there’s a good shot it happens Guy Gardener: Really hoping he doesn’t have the Bruce Wayne head. But it is still nice to see him. Krypto: not sure how they can improve on the previous one, so I’d be fine with that one coming back. A new mold would be cool too. Lex Luthor: probably going to be the 2025 version and I’m happy with that. But I’d love to get a different head for him. Brainiac: probably going to be the New 52 design and I’m cool with that. Mystery character(s): Perry White, Cat Grant, Ron Troupe, and Steve Lombard would all be great additions even if they would just be kitbash. posts.title: [MOC] St. Louis Southwestern - Cotton Belt Route 4-8-4 no. 819
posts.text: "Revolution" I've written before how a locomotive can lie in thought or memory for untold lengths of time, virtually dormant, and then reappear with a strong and captivating force. For me, the Nickel Plate Road 700s are one such example. This is another. Normally I would wax poetic over my connection to a railroad - and I certainly could do that here. That story, however, is better suited for a later date. While part of the connective story is not relevant, what is relevant is the present evolution of my modeling mentality: mainline steam freight railroading. This is a trend that started in earnest in 2022 during the development of 763. With a penchant for the 1940's specifically (in more ways than just Lego), I enjoy representing history. This was the era in which steam was beginning to take its final form in the United States. Steam's finest hour - the core of my modeling. Enter the Cotton Belt Route. The St. Louis Southwestern was a railroad that, as I've described in jest, seemed to enjoy throwing a Consolidation at any problem until a solution was found. They had plenty, along with ten-wheelers and other small motive power. They did roster two breed of 4-8-2, which were secured secondhand from the Florida East Coast and Rock Island to supplement passenger and freight service respectively. The Cotton Belt management, cognizant of the ideas of both efficiency and physical plant, presented the Baldwin engineers with their situation: a new, efficient, more powerful class was needed. The Baldwin engineers returned two proposals: #62784 and #62948. The latter was the winner, and a derivative thereof was ultimately chosen. The first 4-8-4 came to the Cotton Belt in September 1930. Rated for a mere 18% more tractive effort over the latest consolidation from seven years prior, the 800s were capable of handling 30% more tonnage and higher speed. These new engines got the job done. This is perhaps an understatement, as the railroad placed an order for five build-your-own copies to be assembled in their Pine Bluff shops, and included provision for various upgrades over the original Baldwins. The Cotton Belt repeated this internal order in 1942 - and finally our star enters the story. 819 was assembled in late 1942 and early 1943 - the boiler coming from Baldwin, and the shop forces taking five to six weeks to put everything together. 819, the last and largest locomotive built in Arkansas, first ran on February 8, 1943 - a war baby through and through. With such a fascinating backstory, I wish there was more to say about the service life of 819 specifically, but we can safely assume a successful career. These engines ran farther across the system as it was upgraded to handle them, initially running between Tyler and Pine Bluff, then expanding to Shreveport and East St. Louis. The 800s are known for handling the famed Blue Streak Merchandise freight trains, and for handling bridge traffic from the Southern Pacific through Corsicana, including perishables. These details are best told by David Morgan in the November, 1949 issue of Trains Magazine. Strapac's book on Cotton Belt motive power also makes specific note of the railroad using their 800s to handle wartime oil traffic, keeping same off the Gulf and thus less vulnerable to U-boat attacks. As the curtain fell for steam across the country, a handful of L-1s found delayed retirement working for the Southern Pacific. 819 was not among them. The railroad donated the swan song of the Pine Bluff Shops to the city that built it, and the engine became a static park fixture on July 22, 1955. This was not the end. In the Summer of 1982, conversations began between interested parties regarding a new future for 819 - including Cotton Belt employees. This renewed interest, combined with 66 original blueprints for the L-1 gathered from a former Cotton Belt Road Foreman of Engines, led to the creation of the Cotton Belt Railroad Historical Society, which held its first meeting in October 1983. posts.title: Lego Blockly: Graphical Common Programming Environment Web App (Using Intuitive Blockly) for All Lego Robotic Platforms.
posts.text: I decided to go with the irsend repeat count and tried with 2 repeat counts for a total of 3 frames per command. The additionnal delay is awful. Anyway, I implemented Compile Flags at the beginning of the sketches to let you configure what repeat Frame counts you want for your project. Defaults is 2 for PF IR (3 frames) and 0 for PF RF (1 frame) You can also disable PF IR TX, IR RX, or RF TX when you are not using them in your projects. You will find in https://github.com/BlissCA/lego-blockly/tree/dev/SketchArduino, a sketch for ESP-WROOM-32 and one for ESP32-C3. For ESP32: LegoPFIR_BLE_ESP_WROOM_32_V8 I DID clean up and removed previous versions. If you plan to use only RF, then you should set PF IR repeat count to 0 or disable PF IR TX. The delays of both PF IR and PF RF adds up so just disable or reduce at least the repeat frame count of unused features. EDIT: Actually, the response time for one command once in a while is not bad, the IR receiver will probably get the first frame and executes it. The other frames will just do nothing. But it you have 2 consecutives commands, for example, Turn motor ON fwd on Red port and Turn motor ON Rev on Blue port, the ESP32 bridge will first send 5 complete frames for first command and only after that, it will send the 5 frames of second command. So rather than seeing your 2 motors turning on at the same time, there will be about 0.5 to 1 sec delay between each action. Now I'm experimenting sending frames using interleave method. This will be more efficient for sure. Stay tuned :-) EDIT 2: Interleave method is implemented now and it is MUCH more efficient for consecutive commands with multipe frames per commands (which should not happen often). Interleave means, if we repeat 3 command frames for each command, if the ESP bridge receives 2 commands at the same time from blockly, the bridge willl send Cmd1 Frame1, Cmd2 Frame 1, Cmd1 Frame 2, Cmd2 Frame2, Cmd1 Frame3, Cmd2 Frame3... Rather than Cmd1 Frame1, Cmd1 Frame2, Cmd1 Frame 3, Cmd2 Frame1, Cmd2 Frame2, Cmd2 Frame 3.

posts.title: Help with identifying parts/sets!
posts.text: Hi John, what a great find! I’ve done some digging. Samsonite distributed LEGO in Canada until 1988, which explains the bilingual box. The odd thing is that “65” doesn’t match any 1978 set I can find. In the Samsonite listings, 065 is an unrelated 1960s Garage Door set, so yours may simply never have been catalogued. Canadian sets often had their own numbers, different from the European versions with similar box pictures. A couple of suggestions: The member LEGO Historian has researched Canadian Samsonite sets in depth and has scans of the Canadian catalogues from 1976 onwards. It might be worth tagging or messaging him. To get it registered, Brickset and BrickLink both accept new set submissions. Clear photos of all box sides, plus the piece list or instructions if you have them, will help a lot. Would love to know what you find out!

posts.title: So, what Do people want?

Make it easy to finish them: Every part in a set’s inventory actually available to buy, at a sensible price, for years after the set retires. Older instructions and inventories kept online forever. They’re brilliant now, and I hope that never changes. Part numbers printed or moulded somewhere visible, or an official way to identify a loose part, as anyone who’s sorted a job lot knows the pain.
